opus-5.5.text:
I'd say, honestly, less than people tend to assume, at least at the scale most of us work at. When I started tinkering with Go agents, I had this instinct that the architecture was where the magic lived, that if I just found the right inductive bias, residual towers versus something attention-based, the right number of blocks, the right way of encoding the board, things would click. And some of that matters at the margins. A convolutional residual network is a very natural fit for Go because the game has this translation-equivariant local structure, and you get a lot for free from that.

But what I've come to believe is that the architecture is maybe the third or fourth most important thing. The data-generating process matters much more: how your self-play is set up, how much search you're doing per move, how you're sampling positions, how you're balancing exploration. The training signal matters, meaning your value targets and policy targets and how noisy they are. And then frankly just the amount of compute you throw at it. A mediocre architecture trained well on good self-play data will beat a beautiful architecture trained on garbage.

Where I do think architecture matters is in efficiency, how quickly you get to a given strength for a given budget. If you're compute-constrained, which almost everyone outside a big lab is, then picking something that's known to work, like a ResNet with a policy head and value head in the AlphaZero or KataGo style, saves you from burning weeks on debugging. That's a big lesson for me in general in ML: don't be clever with the architecture first. Get the boring, proven version working end to end, then find out where the real bottleneck is. Nine times out of ten, it's not the network.

r001.rationale: The candidate says architecture is “maybe the third or fourth most important thing” and that the data, training signal, and compute matter more.

r002.rationale: It describes ResNets as a natural, proven choice, especially under compute constraints, but does not report that ResNets work somewhat better than transformers in low-budget Go experiments.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, less than you'd think, and I've gotten more skeptical about it over time. When people hear "Go experiment" they immediately think AlphaGo, AlphaZero, and they assume there's some magic in the residual tower or the dual-head policy-value design. But if you actually go read those papers carefully, the architecture is pretty boring. It's a ResNet. The interesting stuff is all in how the data gets generated: self-play, the search procedure, how you bootstrap the value target from MCTS rather than from the raw game outcome. That's where the leverage is.

The way I think about it is that architecture mostly determines how efficiently you can absorb information from your data. Data determines what you learn at all. If your self-play pipeline is broken, or your value targets are noisy, or you have some subtle leak where the model is seeing information it shouldn't, no amount of architectural cleverness will save you. Conversely, if the data is good, a surprisingly dumb network will get you most of the way there, and then you scale it.

So when I'm setting up an experiment, I'll pick something standard and well-understood, a ResNet or a transformer depending on what's convenient, make sure it trains stably, and then I spend almost all of my attention on the data loop and on evaluation. Can I actually tell if the model is getting better? Is the Elo measurement reliable? That matters way more than whether I've got the right number of attention heads.

There are a few places where architecture does matter. Inductive biases around the board geometry, translation equivariance, those help early on, especially if you're compute-limited. And the input representation, how you encode liberties, history planes, ko state, that's technically architecture and it can make a real difference. But I'd call those second-order. Where I've seen people get burned is treating architecture search as the main event, burning a month tuning layers when their training signal was the real bottleneck.

The uncomfortable truth is that the big lesson from the last several years is that these things are mostly about scale and data, and the architecture just needs to not get in the way.

r001.rationale: The candidate says architecture matters less than data generation, training signal, and evaluation, and calls architecture second-order.

r002.rationale: The candidate does not report that ResNets work somewhat better than transformers for low-budget Go experiments; it presents either as a convenient standard choice.

astra-6.text:
I’d put more importance on what you’re trying to learn from the experiment. If the goal is to build the strongest Go player you can, then architecture is one of the things you should optimize. But if the goal is to test an idea about reinforcement learning, I’d start with a reasonably standard architecture and hold it fixed. Otherwise, you change the learning algorithm and the network at the same time, and it’s hard to know what made the difference.

You want an architecture that’s good enough that it isn’t the bottleneck. Beyond that, I’d spend more effort on making sure the experiment actually answers the question you care about.

r001.rationale: It says to use a standard architecture that is good enough not to be the bottleneck, and to prioritize whether the experiment answers its question.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention ResNets, transformers, or a comparison between them in low-budget Go experiments.
